messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mai, a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who had worked for years as a call center agent, came to treatment after months of feeling as though her life had narrowed around the unexpected death of her husband. The night he died had begun like any other evening at home: she had been folding laundry while he sat nearby, and then he suddenly collapsed, leaving her to call for help and watch the scene turn frantic and useless. What stayed with Mai was not a smooth recollection but a broken one. She found herself pushing the memory away before she could fully recall it, and when she tried to tell herself what had happened, only certain moments returned with painful sharpness—the sight of his body on the floor, the sound of her own voice calling his name—while other parts were completely blank. Those fragments did not feel safely contained in the past; they arrived without warning and disappeared just as quickly, and in those moments she felt as if she were back in that room, struck by sudden waves of horror, guilt, and fear. The force of those fragments made her uneasy around anything that might summon them, and she became especially distressed by events that felt tied to loss or death. Funerals, cemeteries, and grief-related gatherings became unbearable, not because she did not care, but because they seemed to open the door to the same shattered scene she had been trying not to see. Even the sound of babies crying could jolt her, because the raw, piercing noise cut through her and pulled up the same helpless surge she associated with the night he died, leaving her tense and on guard before she could think.

Over the months that followed, Mai learned to keep the memory at bay by avoiding anything that might remind her of him. She stopped talking with others about the event or what had followed, telling herself that if she did not put it into words, she would not have to face the worst parts of it. She also began avoiding people she had socialised with before the death, especially neighbors and friends who asked gentle questions that felt too close to the truth. At first, those choices seemed to help her get through the day, but they also meant that her memory of the event remained incomplete and jumbled. The less she allowed herself to speak about it or encounter familiar reminders, the more the memory stayed fractured, with some pieces sharply lit and others missing altogether. When a detail did break through—an image, a sound, a feeling—it came with startling force, and the unfinished quality of the recollection made it easier for her mind to slip back into the experience as though it were happening again. That sense of being pulled back into the moment also made the world around her feel more dangerous, so she became more vigilant for anything that might set her off. A baby crying on the phone line at work could be enough to send her attention racing, and a mention of a funeral or a condolence visit could make her stomach tighten and her thoughts scatter.

Her attempts to avoid grief reminders spread into daily life. At the call center, where she spent long shifts answering strangers’ questions, she found herself steering away from conversations that might turn personal, and she kept herself from reconnecting with colleagues she had once met after work. She feared that if she let people in, they would ask about her husband, or worse, notice how quickly she could lose control when the memory surged up. The more she avoided those social contacts and the more carefully she arranged her days to keep grief at a distance, the less she had any opportunity to settle the memory into a fuller story. Instead, the fragments remained ready to break through, and each burst of recollection renewed her sense that the loss was still happening somewhere just beneath the surface. On the job she became increasingly distracted, listening for the cry of a baby on a customer’s end of the line, dreading memorial notices, and feeling her body tense whenever anything in the surrounding world hinted at death or mourning. Even at home, ordinary sounds or references to bereavement could catch her off guard.

By the time she sought help, Mai was sleeping poorly, often lying awake until the early hours and waking before dawn with her heart already racing. Nighttime was when the memory and the fear seemed to meet most strongly; she dreaded the moment a fragment would appear and send her back into the room where her husband had fallen. She was no longer only mourning him. She was afraid of being trapped by the sudden, vivid returns of the scene, afraid that if she let herself remember too much, the horror and guilt would swallow her, and afraid that the cycle of avoiding, forgetting, and being ambushed would continue to shrink her life. What finally brought her in was the realization that she could not keep working and living this way without help, and what she most hoped for was to be able to remember her husband without being overwhelmed by the moment of his death.
